On the underside of each engine is a two large drum around which is wound a stout cable and when the engine is in motion the plough is drawn from one side of the field to the other. To draw the plough back to the other side the engine on the far side is used.

BLUE GRASS PROFITS,

Growing wild in its native environment and costing nothing to raise, the seed of the famous Blue Grass of Central Kentucky nets the farmer a neat little profit at harvesting time. The nature of this grass is such that cattle can be raised and fattened on it the year round without destroying the seed. The seed which is merely a by product of grass used for grazing purposes and seldom raised especially for marketing when harvested sells in good years for an average of $325,00. Profit realized from this source alone on many of the large stock farms of Central Kentucky sometimes runs into thousands of dollars. Blue grass seed is in demand all over the United States and Europe for lawns and pasturage. In recent years the increase of golf courses in this country, which are almost all seeded with blue grass has greatly increased the demand for this seed. 6/21/22

AN AUTOMATIC PIOW

C:25363 An automatic plow is the /atest. All the farmer has to do is to wind it up, so to speak, supply it with gasoline, and start it out upon the expanse of field to be plowed. The manless plow was invented by Prof. J.B. Davidson of the Iowa State College at Ames. The device consists of a two wheel tractor with a four horse power, single cylinder engine to furnish the power. Right and left hand plow bottoms are attached to the frame with their beams opposite and nearly at right angle to the tractor axle and so place that while one plow is in service the other is carried above the surface of the soil. This new invention is considered the greatest boon to the farmer in the way of labor saving devices that so far has been devised.

NEW YORK.
Vincent Astor and a gas tractor on his experiment farm hauling six 14-inch plows, a cutaway disc harrow and pulverizer.

Rinebeck, N. Y., July 7.—Owners of farms located for hundred miles around this vicinity are anxiously awaiting the first news of the result of experiments on the six hundred acres of virgin soil on the estate of young Vincent Astor, which he set aside for a truck farm. The beautiful stretch of land was turned into a farm inside of thirty days by the huge agricultural machines Mr. Astor ordered from the West. The 60 horse power caterpillar gas tractor hauled six 14-inch gang plows, behind to which was attached a cutaway disc harrow with six rows of revolving discs, 14 discs to to the row, and behind that a 14-foot, 3-section pulverizer, These machines at one working converted the virgin sod into pulverized soil, ready to plant, at an average speed of 20 acres a day. As fast as the soil was prepared it was planted, so that the time the plowing was done crops were already up over a large part of the surface.

Prince Rupert, B. C., July 6.—Accompanied only by two Indian guides Miss Mary L. Jobe, professor of history in the Normal College of New York city, will on Wednesday start from Prince Rupert on a long trip into the unexplored wilds of Northern British Columbia and Southeastern Alaska. Miss Jobe is the veteran of several explorations into the Selkirk Mountains of this district. She said the purpose of her present trip is largely ethmological; that she expected to make a study of the traditions, ceremonies, habits and language of the Athabascaan or "Carrier" tribe of Indians along the Skeena and Peace rivers. The only knowledge of this tribe has been brought by trappers from the Hudson Bay trading posts. She will be ten weeks away from civilization and expects to discover some tribes that have never been seen by a white man.
Bulgarians Nearing Vrania, Says Report.
Indications Are That Serbs and Greeks Are Suffering Defeat at Hand of the Bulgars—Powers Are Making No Efforts to Stop War
OFFICIAL REPORTS SCARCE

London, July 7.—The most important news from the seat of war to-day is the report, confirmed from Sofia, of the appearance of a large Bulgarian force at Vrania, threatening the Servian line of retreat.
The wounded describe the battles as almost inhuman in their ferocity, the men throwing away their firearms and using their bayonets as daggers.

Still more significant, as tending to confirm the belief that the Servians are suffering defeat, is the announcement from Belgrade that only meager reports are being received from the Servian army headquarters and that the government has decided to publish reports only on alternate days. In addition a rigorous censorship on the newspapers is being enforced.

Whatever the policy of the European powers may be, little is now heard of attempts to stop the war. The ambassador conferences met in London again to-day, but apparently did little else than discuss the boundaries of Albania. Meanwhile, Rumania and Turkey give signs that they will not long be idle spectators.
News of the fighting continues to be of a contradictory character. It is almost invariably from official sources in the respective capitals; no independent testimony is available.
This applies equally to the struggle between the Greeks and the Bulgarians and between the Servians and Bulgarians.

A dispatch from Saloniki reports that the Greeks have occupied Demirhishir and Strumitza, and according to the most likely information the Bulgarian general, Ivanoff, is slowly retiring before the superior Greek forces northward since his army was weakened by the departure of his right wing to attack Krivolak.
